That same afternoon, during Sara's absence, something unusual took place in the attic. Melchisedec alone witnessed it. So frightened and bewildered was he that he scurried home to his hole and hid. There he actually shook and trembled, peering out with furtive caution to discover what was happening.

Since Sara's departure early that morning, the attic had been silent except for rain tapping on the roof slates and skylight. Melchisedec had found it rather boring. When even the rain stopped and the silence became complete, he decided to venture out and investigate, although experience told him Sara would not be back for a while. He wandered, sniffing, and had just discovered a completely unexpected crumb, unaccountably left over from his previous meal, when a noise on the roof caught his attention. Heart beating fast, he stood perfectly still, listening. Something seemed to be moving up there. It came towards the skylight and reached it. Mysteriously, the skylight began to open. A dark face looked down into the attic, and another face appeared behind it. Both watched with careful interest. Two men were outside, quietly preparing to climb through the opening. They were Ram Dass and the Indian gentleman's young secretary, though Melchisedec naturally knew nothing of that. All he knew was that men were violating the attic's quiet privacy. As the dark-faced one lowered himself through the window with such effortless skill that he made no sound, the rat turned and raced for his hole. He was terrified. He had stopped being afraid of Sara: she threw only crumbs and made only soft, low, coaxing whistles. Strange men, however, were dangerous company. Crouched flat just inside his home, he could barely manage to look through the crack with one bright, anxious eye. I cannot say how much of their talk he understood. Even if he had understood every word, he would probably still have been thoroughly puzzled.
Young and lightly built, the secretary followed through the skylight as quietly as Ram Dass. He caught one last glimpse of Melchisedec's tail disappearing.
In a whisper he asked Ram Dass, "Was that a rat?"
Ram Dass whispered back, "A rat, yes, Sahib. A great many live inside these walls."
"Ugh!" said the young man. "How is the child not frightened out of her wits by them?"
Ram Dass moved his hands in a gesture and gave a respectful smile. Though Sara had spoken to him only once, he stood there as someone who knew her intimately and could explain her nature.

"Sahib, this child befriends everything," he replied. "She differs from other children. Often I see her without her seeing me. Many nights I cross the slates to make sure she is safe. From my window I watch when she has no idea I am nearby. On that table she stands gazing at the sky, as though it has words for her. When she calls, the sparrows answer. Loneliness has led her to feed and tame the rat. The poor slave who works in this house seeks comfort here. A little child visits secretly, and an older one who adores her would listen for ever if allowed. Crossing the roof, I have seen it all. The mistress here is a wicked woman and treats her like a pariah. Yet she carries herself like a child with royal blood in her veins!"
"You've learned a great deal about her, it seems," remarked the secretary.

"I know the life she leads each day," Ram Dass answered. "I know when she leaves and returns, what makes her sad, and her few poor pleasures. I know her hunger and her cold. I know the nights she studies alone over her books until midnight, and the times her hidden friends creep in and make her happy, as children can be happy even in poverty. Their coming lets her whisper, laugh, and talk. If illness came to her, I should know that too, and if it could be managed I would come to tend her."
"You're certain nobody else comes anywhere near this place, and that she won't return to catch us? Finding us in her room would frighten her and ruin Sahib Carrisford's plan."
Without a sound, Ram Dass went over and stationed himself beside the door.
"Only she comes up here, Sahib," he assured him. "She went out carrying her basket and may be absent for hours. Here by the door I will hear footsteps before they reach the final staircase."
From his breast pocket the secretary drew a pencil and a writing tablet.
"Listen carefully," he told him. Then he began a slow, quiet circuit of the miserable little attic, making quick notes as he examined its contents.
He started with the narrow bed, testing the mattress with his hand and giving an exclamation.

"Hard as stone," he said. "One day while she's away we'll have to change this. Bringing a mattress across will need a special trip; tonight won't be possible." He turned back the bedclothes and inspected the single thin pillow.

"A grubby, worn coverlet, a thin blanket, patched and ragged sheets," he observed. "What a bed to put a child in, especially in a supposedly respectable house!" His eyes moved to the rusty fireplace. "That grate hasn't held a fire in a very long time."
"Not once in all the time I have watched it," Ram Dass replied. "This house's mistress does not consider that anyone besides herself might feel cold."
Writing rapidly, the secretary filled his tablet. He looked up, tore away one sheet, and tucked it into his breast pocket.
"An unusual way to go about things," he remarked. "Whose idea was it?"
Ram Dass bowed with modest, almost apologetic deference.

"The first idea was mine, Sahib, though only a fancy," he admitted. "I am fond of the little one. We are lonely, both of us. She tells her secret friends the visions she imagines. One night, feeling sad myself, I lay by the open skylight and listened. She described how this wretched room might look if it were comfortable. As she spoke she seemed to see it, and the words made her warmer and happier. Then she imagined this plan. Next day the Sahib was ill and miserable, and I repeated it to entertain him. It was only a dream then, yet it pleased him. Hearing what the child did amused him. He grew interested and began asking questions. At last the idea of turning her visions into actual things became a pleasure to him."

"Do you really think you can manage it while she's asleep? What if she wakes?" the secretary asked. Whatever this scheme was, it had plainly caught his imagination and pleased him as much as it had Sahib Carrisford.

Ram Dass answered, "My feet can be as quiet as velvet. Children sleep deeply, even unhappy children. Many times I could have entered at night without making her turn her head on the pillow. If the other bearer hands everything through the skylight, I can arrange it all without waking her. She will open her eyes and believe a magician has visited."
His smile suggested a heart growing warm beneath the white robe, and the secretary returned it.
"Like something from the Arabian Nights," he said. "Only an Oriental could have dreamed this up. A plan like that doesn't belong among London's fogs."

Their visit was short, much to Melchisedec's relief. Probably understanding none of their words, he found their whispering and movements threatening. The young secretary appeared interested in every detail. His notes covered the floor, fireplace, damaged footstool, old table, and walls. He repeatedly ran his hand over the last, looking especially pleased to discover old nails driven in here and there.
"They'll do for hanging things," he said.
A mysterious smile crossed Ram Dass's face.

"Yesterday I came while she was away," he explained. "I brought small, sharp nails that press into plaster without hammering. Wherever I might need one, I put it in. Many are now waiting in the walls."
Standing still, the Indian gentleman's secretary surveyed the room once more and slipped his tablet back into his pocket.
"That should be enough notes. We can leave now," he said. "Sahib Carrisford has a generous heart. What a terrible pity he still hasn't found that missing child."
"Finding her would bring back his strength," said Ram Dass. "Perhaps his God will yet guide her to him."

They climbed out as silently as they had entered. Only when Melchisedec was absolutely certain they had gone did relief take hold. A few minutes later he judged it safe to leave his hole and scuffle about again. After all, even such terrifying human beings might have carried crumbs in their pockets and accidentally dropped one or two on the floor.
